common_name: Pop Star Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Lacecap Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pop Star is an Endless Summer series hydrangea bred for a compact, genetically dwarf habit and lacecap (rather than mophead) flowers that bloom reliably on both old and new wood.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade in hot climates. Pop Star is part of the Endless Summer series but breaks from its mophead siblings with lacy, floriferous lacecap flower clusters in electric blue or bright pink depending on soil pH, held on a genetically compact plant that stays tidy in borders and containers without heavy pruning. It flowers on both old wood carried over from the previous season and new wood produced the same year, so winter dieback or a late frost that damages old stems does not prevent a strong rebloom through summer and fall. Keep soil consistently moist, since the plant's heavy flower production increases water demand, and limit pruning to shaping and removal of dead wood in late winter to preserve the old-wood buds that provide the earliest flush.
sources: Bailey Nurseries — Endless Summer Series: Pop Star Hydrangea

common_name: Quick Fire Fab Hydrangea (Larger-Flowered Improved Quick Fire Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Quick Fire Fab is an improved sport of Quick Fire bred for larger, denser, football-shaped flower panicles with distinctive x-shaped florets on the same early-blooming, sun-tolerant plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Quick Fire Fab improves on the original Quick Fire with larger, denser, football-shaped panicles made up of densely packed, uniquely x-shaped florets that open creamy white and age from the base upward through pink to deep red as the season progresses, extending the color display earlier than other panicle hydrangeas. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood, so a hard renewal pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the season's flowers. It is among the most sun-tolerant hydrangeas and, once established, handles heat and drier soil better than mophead types, making it a good choice for larger sunny borders or as a small specimen tree when trained to a single trunk.

common_name: Let's Dance Sky View Hydrangea (Continuous-Blooming Compact Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Let's Dance Sky View is a Proven Winners continuous-blooming bigleaf hydrangea that sets flower buds along the entire length of each stem rather than just at the tips, so winter dieback or pruning does not eliminate a season's bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun in cool climates or partial shade in warmer regions. Let's Dance Sky View is bred to flower continuously rather than just repeat late in the season, setting buds all along the stem instead of only at the tips, so even a plant that dies back to the ground over winter or is pruned hard will still produce flowers the same year. Its compact, tidy habit and thick, glossy foliage suit foundation plantings, borders, and containers. Flowers open sky blue with a honeydew-green eye in acidic soil and shift toward lavender or pink in more alkaline soil, sometimes showing more than one shade on the same plant; color can be nudged bluer with soil sulfur or aluminum sulfate amendments. Prune only lightly to shape and remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes developing flower buds.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Reblooming Hydrangea Cultivars
